questions.question: How do you iterate over a string in Go, and what do you get each iteration?
questions.title: String Iteration
questions.direct_answer: for i, r := range s — i is a BYTE OFFSET, r is the decoded RUNE (code point). The offset advances by each rune's width (1-4 bytes). For byte-level iteration: a classic loop with s[i], or range []byte(s).

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    LOOP[for i, r := range s] --> DEC[decode at i]
    DEC --> Y[i=byte offset, r=rune]
    Y --> ADV[i += width - jumps past wide runes]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The decoder behind range: each iteration reads the current byte, infers the width from its leading bits (UTF-8 is self-synchronizing forward), gathers the bytes, decodes, returns (offset, rune). O(n) total, O(1) per rune, no allocation — decoding in registers.

Why byte-offset (not rune-index) for the first return: s[start:end] slices by BYTES, and range's i is exactly where each rune starts — substring building from iteration output composes directly: for i, r := range s { if r == target { return s[i:] } }. A rune-index loop can't slice without recomputing offsets.

The invalid-UTF-8 case: a Go string CAN hold arbitrary bytes. range handles invalid sequences by yielding U+FFFD (replacement character) with width 1 — no panic, no stop. That makes range safe over ANY string — and explains why byte and rune loops can disagree on corrupt input's count.

The two real-world jobs the two modes map to: structure scanning (delimiters, patterns) wants byte offsets (found positions slice cleanly); character logic (rendering, case, width) wants runes. range gives both — which is why it's the loop.

questions.question: What is the difference between ranging over a string and a slice of runes?
questions.title: When would you use String Iteration in a real project
questions.direct_answer: range s decodes runes on the fly (no allocation, byte offsets). range []rune(s) iterates a materialized int32 slice (one allocation, rune indices). Use range s unless you need random rune access or repeated passes.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: range s decodes runes on the fly (no allocation, byte offsets). range []rune(s) iterates a materialized int32 slice (one allocation, rune indices). Use range s unless you need random rune.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Both yield runes — the difference is where the runes live:

```go
// range over the string — decoded on the fly, zero allocation
for i, r := range s { ... }        // i = byte offset

// range over the materialized slice — one allocation, done
rs := []rune(s)
for i, r := range rs { ... }      // i = slice index (== rune index)
```

The string range decodes each rune in registers as it walks — nothing is stored. The slice range iterates an int32 array that was fully built (O(n) allocation, decode pass already paid).

When the materialized version is right: (1) you need rune indices, not byte offsets (the i differs — byte offsets skip past wide runes); (2) you need MULTIPLE passes (sort the runes, reverse, scan twice — one decode, many iterations); (3) you need random access (rs[k] for various k). For any of those, []rune(s) once, then work the slice.

When the string range is right: everything else — single pass, no stored runes, no allocation. The common waste: []rune(s) inside a function called per-item — the conversion allocates every call when a range (or a single pass with utf8 functions) needed nothing stored.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    RS[range s] --> |on-the-fly decode| Z[no alloc - byte offsets]
    MS[range rune s] --> |materialized| M[one alloc - rune indices]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The cost anatomy: range s — zero allocation, the decode is arithmetic per rune (the leading-bits width inference + a small lookup), total O(n) CPU. []rune(s) — the same decode walk PLUS an allocation (4 bytes per rune — 4x the string's byte count for ASCII input) plus the writes. The first pass over the slice is then pure iteration (cheaper per step than string decoding — the work was front-loaded). Break-even: one pass — string range wins (no alloc); many passes or indexed access — the slice wins (amortize the materialization).

The index-semantic difference, one layer down: string range's i is a byte offset — it's what slicing needs (s[i:] works immediately). []rune range's i is a rune index — it's what character arithmetic needs (rs[k:] gives the k-th character onward, not the k-th byte onward). The two 'indices' answer different questions, and picking the iteration form is really picking which index your logic needs.

The interop with the slice-tricks family: []rune materialization is what unlocks rune-level slice operations — reverse (swap ends), filter runes (even runes), dedupe characters. The byte equivalents corrupt multibyte runes (the reverse demonstration from the rune-vs-byte topic). The pattern: convert once, operate as a slice, convert back once — the batch-then-convert discipline, identical in shape to the Builder amortization.

questions.question: Why does iterating with s[i] in a classic for loop give wrong characters for non-ASCII strings?
questions.title: a common mistake when using String Iteration
questions.direct_answer: s[i] is a BYTE — for multi-byte runes, the loop yields encoding fragments (195, 169 for é), not characters. Comparing s[i] to a rune literal never matches. Use range for characters, or utf8.DecodeRuneInString for manual walking.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: s[i] is a BYTE — for multi-byte runes, the loop yields encoding fragments (195, 169 for é), not characters. Comparing s[i] to a rune literal never matches. Use range for.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The classic loop is byte iteration — correct for its actual unit, wrong when read as characters:

```go
s := "héllo"
for i := 0; i < len(s); i++ {
    fmt.Println(s[i])   // 104, 195, 169, 108, 108, 111
}
// s[1] == 'é'  — false: s[1] is 195 (a byte), 'é' is 233 (a rune)
```

The bug shape: the loop LOOKS right on ASCII test data (every byte is a character), ships, and produces silently wrong behavior on the first international input — comparisons never match, counts are inflated, output corrupts when bytes are reassembled.

The correct forms, by need:

```go
for i, r := range s { ... }              // runes, free
r, size := utf8.DecodeRuneInString(s[i:])  // manual walk — r, its width
```

The DecodeRuneInString pattern is the bridge when you need the classic loop's control (explicit bounds, early exit with position) but rune semantics — it returns (rune, byte-width), you advance i by size yourself. It's how the stdlib's own string functions are written.

The interview diagnosis: any classic loop over a string doing comparisons against character literals, or accumulating bytes into output, is suspect on sight — the question is 'what happens on é?' and the answer for s[i]-based code is 'corruption.'

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B[byte loop over helo] --> F[195 169 - e in FRAGMENTS]
    F --> CMP[s i == rune e never matches]
    R[range] --> DE[233 - the actual rune]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the byte fragment is 195 and 169 specifically: é (U+00E9, decimal 233) encodes as two UTF-8 bytes — 0xC3 0xA9 (195, 169). The first byte (110xxxxx) marks a 2-byte sequence; the second (10xxxxxx) is the continuation. A byte loop stops at each — and s[1] (195) compares against 'é' (the rune constant 233) as uint8-vs-int32... never equal (even ignoring width, 195 ≠ 233 — the byte ISN'T the code point).

The silent-corruption path, end to end: a loop building output via s[i] appends the same bytes — so echoing input 'works' (bytes preserved). The corruption appears at COMPARISON and CHARACTER logic: counting vowels (each é counts 0 — no byte equals 'e' or 'é'), validating ('é' rejected as non-alpha — 195 and 169 both fail the test), or indexing by character count (position 2 is mid-rune). The bugs are logic bugs, not data loss — which makes them intermittent and test-resistant (ASCII tests pass).

The stdlib's own bridge functions, worth naming as the expert answer: utf8.DecodeRuneInString(s[i:]) — next rune + width from position i (the manual-walk primitive); strings.Map — rune-wise transform without explicit indices (the function gets each rune; positions are handled); utf8.RuneCountInString — the count when the loop's only job was length. Every one of these replaces a byte-loop idiom with the rune-correct equivalent — and code review treats the classic-loop-over-string-with-comparisons pattern as a finding, not a style choice.

questions.question: How do you find the position of a character or substring in a Go string?
questions.title: compare String Iteration with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: strings.Index(s, substr) — byte offset of the first occurrence, -1 if absent. For a single rune: strings.IndexRune. For any of a set: IndexAny. All return byte offsets — compose directly with slicing.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: strings.Index(s, substr) — byte offset of the first occurrence, -1 if absent. For a single rune: strings.IndexRune. For any of a set: IndexAny. All return byte offsets — compose directly.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The Index family, all returning byte offsets (or -1):

```go
strings.Index("hello", "l")        // 2 — first "l"
strings.Index("hello", "lo")       // 3 — substring works
strings.Index("hello", "z")        // -1
strings.IndexRune("héllo", 'é')    // 1 — é's byte offset
strings.IndexAny("hello", "oe")    // 1 — first of any
strings.LastIndex("hello", "l")    // 3 — from the right
```

Executed. The -1 convention: every search returns -1 for absent (never an error, never a bool) — the caller's check is if idx >= 0 or idx != -1, and the classic split idiom is idx := strings.Index(s, ":"); if idx < 0 { not found } else { key, val := s[:idx], s[idx+1:] }.

The byte-offset design: results compose with slicing — found positions slice cleanly. The rune relationship: IndexRune gives the BYTE offset OF a rune — searching for 'é' returns 1 (where its 2 bytes start), not rune-index 1. Both units live together: search in bytes, count in runes when needed.

The contains-vs-index relationship: strings.Contains(s, sub) is Index(s, sub) >= 0 — the boolean wrapper, same machinery. Use Contains when you don't need WHERE; Index when you do.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    ID[Index - byte offset or -1]
    IDR[IndexRune - byte offset OF a rune]
    C[Contains == Index >= 0]
    CU[Cut - before, after, found]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The implementation tiering: Index uses an optimized search (the runtime's search handles the small-pattern cases with fast paths — the simple byte scan for 1-byte needles, a two-way/Rabin-Karp-flavored approach for longer ones). IndexRune delegates to Index(s, string(r)) for multibyte runes — or a single-byte scan for ASCII-width runes. IndexByte is the raw primitive the others bottom out in. The API surface is conveniences over three primitives — byte, rune, substring — and each exists because the caller's needle is naturally one of the three.

The composable idiom this family enables — the parser's bread and butter: Index + slice, chained. Find separator, split there; find the next, split again; the 'walk the string by found positions' pattern. strings.Cut (Go 1.18) formalized the single most common instance: Cut(s, sep) returns (before, after, found) — the Index-plus-slice-with-a-name that replaces the four-line idiom. Before Cut, every parser hand-wrote it; the stdlib watched the pattern and promoted it — API evolution in miniature.

The case-insensitive and pattern boundaries: EqualFold for case-insensitive equality (no case-insensitive Index in the stdlib — fold both sides, or use a regexp with (?i)); regexp for pattern positions (submatch indices — the general tool at ~10-50x the cost). The tiers, restated: bytes/rune/substring (Index family — fast, literal), case-folded (manual or strings.EqualFold for equality only), pattern (regexp — general, slow). Choosing by needle-expressiveness is the discipline.

questions.question: How do you reverse a string in Go?
questions.title: debug a problem involving String Iteration
questions.direct_answer: Convert to []rune(s), swap ends inward, convert back: for i, j := 0, len(r)-1; i < j; i, j = i+1, j-1 { r[i], r[j] = r[j], r[i] }. Reversing BYTES destroys multibyte runes — the rune conversion is mandatory for Unicode-safe reversal.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Convert to []rune(s), swap ends inward, convert back: for i, j := 0, len(r)-1; i < j; i, j = i+1, j-1 { r[i], r[j] = r[j], r[i] }. Reversing.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R[rune + swap ends] --> OK[helo to oleh - e moves as one unit]
    B[byte + swap] --> BAD[invalid UTF-8 - decodes to replacement chars]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The three-unit hierarchy, resurfacing one final time: bytes (storage — what's actually in the string), runes (code points — what []rune gives you), graphemes (user characters — what rune reversal still doesn't give you). The reversal question is a proxy for 'which unit does your string operation work on' — and every string function answer in this whole module has been the same question with a different function.

The corruption anatomy, byte by byte, for the definitive demonstration: "héllo" = [104 195 169 108 108 111]. Byte-reversed: [111 108 108 169 195 104] — the é pair (195 169) became (169 195): the continuation byte (10xxxxxx) now LEADS, which no valid sequence does. A decoder sees 169 (a continuation without a lead), yields U+FFFD, then 195 leads a 2-byte sequence that consumes 104 ('h') as its continuation — also invalid. Two runes destroyed by one swap. That's not abstract: this exact bug pattern appears in every language with UTF-8 + byte-indexed reversal, and Go's answer is the same as its iteration story — the rune is the character unit; say you mean it.

The allocation-conscious variant for interviews (the memory-sensitive follow-up): if reversal is in a hot path, the []rune allocation per call is the cost — the manual alternative is walking with utf8.DecodeRuneInString from both ends simultaneously (forward decoder + backward decoder — UTF-8's backward self-synchronization requires care: DecodeLastRuneInString), swapping into a pre-allocated []byte. Zero rune-slice allocation, byte-level buffer, rune-level semantics — the pattern the stdlib uses internally for its own bidi needs. The readable version remains []rune + swap; the optimized version is a niche answered only when profiling demands it.
